fields.sample_size: doctrinal review of Spanish water legislation from the 1813 provincial instruction through the 1866/1879 Water Laws, the 1985 Water Law, Law 46/1999, RDL 1/2001 and municipal and regional rules; legal methodology with a SWOT (DAFO) analysis; no respondent sample
fields.effect_estimate: Spanish water legislation treats water as a resource, not as a right: the 1985 Water Law and its reforms (Law 46/1999 introducing water markets; RDL 1/2001) regulate public hydraulic domain, quality and planning without recognising a human right to water; municipal law has long obliged councils to supply drinking water and sanitation (e.g. 1924 Royal Decree-law declaring water supply a public service; the current local regime law lets residents demand compliance); autonomous-community statutes include nothing on water governance or the human right (some list it as a citizen right). Competence is split between state, regions and municipalities, producing a 'water war'. The author calls for participatory, multilevel water governance recognising water as a human right.
fields.study_design: doctrinal legal-historical analysis with SWOT (single-country legislative review)

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a legal-territorial analysis of Spanish water legislation (1813-2018), read in full text 2026-10-04. Legislation treats water as a resource rather than a right; municipal supply duties are old and strong; competences are fragmented across levels. Doctrinal; no outcome data.
